A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and contain complete, readable main text, five figures, equations, and Appendices A–C. The material supports a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original numerical demonstrations, including conjugate-model simulations in Figure 4 averaged over 50 random seeds, with settings in Appendix C.

after.justification: v3 retains these original simulations and their reported outcomes in Figure 4 and Appendix C.

M1.justification: The decision-theoretic framework and experimental models remain unchanged. The revision does not specify a new acquisition algorithm, predictive model, or updating procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the Gaussian-process regression demonstration, discrete and continuous conjugate-model simulations, and active learning on Curated MNIST and Coarse ImageNet.

E2.justification: Figure 5 retains the same comparison methods on both datasets: random acquisition, predictive entropy, and BALD. No evaluated comparator is added or removed.

E3.justification: Appendix C retains the same data generation, model settings, losses, and sample sizes. Figure 4 still uses n = 1, 10, 100, 1000 and squared estimation errors; Figure 5 retains test negative log likelihood versus label count.

E4.justification: The loss-dependent Gaussian-process demonstration in Figure 3 and finite-data estimation-error analysis in Figure 4 are retained. No ablation, robustness test, or additional case study is introduced.

E5.justification: Figure 4 and Appendix C.2 report the same averaging over 50 repetitions with different random seeds. No uncertainty-reporting practice or statistical test changes.

E6.justification: Figures 3–5 contain identical plot graphics and retain their findings, including the comparison of short-run and long-run estimation errors and BALD's advantage over predictive-entropy acquisition. No empirical result is added, removed, or corrected.

T1.justification: Section 4 and Figure 2 replace conditional single-observation training entropy with joint training-sequence entropy. Section 3.3 changes the minimax criterion from worst-case loss to worst-case frequentist risk, and Section 5.3 separately denotes the proxy policy as π′. The main propositions and appendix proofs are retained.

C1.justification: The abstract and central contributions remain unchanged. Conclusion (e) now explicitly says BALD estimates long-run reducible predictive uncertainty, matching the scope already stated in v2's introduction and Section 5.5.

C2.justification: Section 5.4 adds an interpretation of expected score as frequentist risk for an outer decision problem and distinguishes this from risk also averaged over training data. Existing limitations concerning imperfect reference distributions and inaccurate uncertainty estimators remain.

D1.justification: Appendix C retains the code-access information, toy datasets, model specifications, kernel, noise setting, and experimental instructions. Figure 3's added description of real-valued inputs and outputs was already available in v2's Appendix C.1.

R1.justification: The minimax discussion and bibliography replace Wald (1949) with two distinct works, Wald (1939) and Wald (1945). The broader related-work coverage and positioning remain unchanged.

P1.justification: There are limited prose revisions throughout the introduction, conceptual discussion, and conclusion, plus a revised Section 3.7 heading and acknowledgements. The section order and appendix organization remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 1 receives clearer group labels, and Figure 2 replaces numbered lists with horizontal groups separated by explicit non-equality symbols. Captions are refined, and Section 5.4 consolidates an equivalent decomposition into annotated Equation 5. Empirical plots remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: The more precise minimax description, added frequentist-risk interpretation in Section 5.4, and clearer Figure 2 improve conceptual precision and readability. These are limited gains: the central claims, proofs, experimental settings, and empirical evidence remain substantially unchanged.
